summary:
Rashi Agrawal (Hinge Health AI/ML lead) frames consumer health AI as unsafe by production baseline, not by frontier-model limits. Three signals ground the claim: a 60-year-old man bromide-poisoned for three months after an AI told him to swap salt with sodium bromide, landing in the ER at 200x the safe level for three weeks; Mount Sinai's first independent consumer health AI safety test showing under-triaging of life-threatening emergencies about 50% of the time; and ECRI naming AI chatbot misuse the #1 health-technology hazard for 2026, with ~40 million people already self-triaging this way.

She builds three non-negotiable architectural foundations. (1) PHI protection: strip protected data at the ingestion pipeline boundary so dashboards contain nothing to redact, with strict production/non-production separation and access gated by role and regulated geographic region, grounded in HIPAA, FDA GMLP, and state laws. (2) Deterministic code above the model: a code layer runs first on every turn and owns irreversible decisions (911/988 escalation, intent routing across capabilities, identity verification), because even frontier labs' root/system/developer/user/guideline hierarchy is one prompt-injection away from override. (3) Continuous evaluation: 30+ automated judges score clinical accuracy, safety, escalation, relevance, drift, and refusal on live traffic; member thumbs feedback and 100%-sampled human review of high-stake traces supply the truth signal; every new production failure becomes a new judge, since fixes regress under new prompts, tools, and model shifts.

Her five-rule launch decisioning framework then resolves architecture-bound stalemates: rule 1, worst-plausible-case sets severity (a 0.1% serious-harm bug outweighs one that lightly annoys 100%); rule 2, never quietly downgrade a bug because you cannot reach it; rule 3, asymmetric defaults (hold and fix safety bugs, ship polish bugs); rule 4, calibrate to revealed, not stated, risk tolerance, since launch bar equals what production already accepts; rule 5, humans are the constraint, because judges scale but pattern interpretation does not, and fast-follows are committed debt, not optional backlog.

She closes with a discipline that must come before any of this: in a non-deterministic system the judge is also non-deterministic, so before trusting a score drop (e.g., 4.9 to 4.5), verify the scorer. Her one-slide summary captures the talk as: don't policy what you can architect, don't prompt what you can code, don't gate what you can monitor; score by worst case, default to the safer mistake, calibrate to the org, and design for the human in the loop. Architecture is how, decisioning is when, member trust is why.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: 40 million people use frontier models to self-triage healthcare, so safety is a production-baseline problem, not a frontier research problem.
PHI should be stripped at the ingestion pipeline boundary so it is never stored, with production/non-production separated and access gated by role and regulated region.
Irreversible decisions (911/988 escalation, intent routing, identity verification) must live in a deterministic code layer that executes before the model on every turn.
Prompts are not security boundaries; even frontier labs' authority hierarchy is one prompt-injection away from override.
Safety runs as continuous live-traffic judging across 30+ automated dimensions, member feedback, and 100%-sampled human review of high-stake cases, not as a pre-launch gate.
Every new production failure becomes a new judge, because fixes regress under new prompts, tools, and model shifts.

Five-rule launch decisioning: worst-case severity, no quiet downgrades, asymmetric defaults (hold safety bugs, ship polish bugs), calibrate to revealed not stated risk tolerance, humans are the constraint.
Before changing an agent on a judge-score drop, first ask whether the judge is right; fixing a judge prompt is not cheating because judges are software that must evolve.
Fast-follows are committed debt, not optional backlog; if it didn't ship at launch, it is already owed.
Design PHI handling so protected data is stripped at ingestion and access is gated by role and regulated region.

sections.title: State of healthcare AI and the 40M self-triage baseline
sections.summary: Rashi introduces herself as Hinge Health's AI/ML lead and frames consumer health AI as unsafe by production baseline. She cites the bromide-poisoning case (60-year-old, 3 months on sodium bromide, ER at 200x safe bromide level, 3-week stay), Mount Sinai's first independent safety test showing ~50% under-triaging of life-threatening emergencies, and ECRI naming AI chatbot misuse the #1 health-technology hazard for 2026, noting ~40 million people already self-triage this way.

sections.title: Three non-negotiable foundations
sections.summary: She previews the talk's structure: (1) the constraint is the architecture, (2) deterministic rules belong above the model, not inside it, and (3) safety is a continuous evaluation layer, not a one-time gate, before introducing a second half on decisioning frameworks when architecture is not enough.

sections.title: Layer 1: PHI at the architecture level
sections.summary: Policy tells you what to protect, architecture makes sure it happens. PHI is stripped at the ingestion pipeline boundary so dashboards never contain data to redact. Production and non-production are fully separated, and access depends on role and regulated geographic region. HIPAA, FDA GMLP, and state laws like Texas Triaga are grounding inputs, not afterthoughts.

sections.title: Layer 2: Deterministic code above the model
sections.summary: A code layer runs first on every turn before the model and owns irreversible decisions. Examples: routing self-harm/suicidal-ideation/acute-emergency turns to 911 or 988 without the model seeing them, deterministic intent routing across clinical, tech support, education, and exercise recommendation capabilities, and authentication as a security boundary before member data. She notes frontier labs' root/system/developer/user/guideline hierarchy is one prompt-injection away from override, so prompts are not security boundaries.

sections.title: Layer 3: Safety as a continuous evaluation layer
sections.summary: Safety is not a pre-launch checklist. Automated judges (30, 40, or more) score clinical accuracy, safety, escalation, relevance, drift, refusal, etc., on live traffic; member thumbs feedback provides the truth signal; and humans review random sample traces with 100% sampling on high-stake cases. Because fixes regress under new prompts, tools, and model shifts, every new production failure becomes a new judge, and monitoring is the first resort, not the last.

sections.title: Layer 4: Five stakeholders, five risks, five days to launch
sections.summary: She sets up a launch-day scenario: one open issue, five days to ship, five stakeholders (clinical, legal, compliance, product, engineering) each seeing a different risk with a different fix. She introduces the first two of five decisioning rules: rule 1, worst-plausible case sets severity (a 0.1% serious-harm bug outweighs one that lightly annoys 100%); rule 2, severity is not capacity, so the three options are fix, delay, or accept with explicit sign-off.

sections.title: Rules 3-5: asymmetric defaults, revealed risk tolerance, humans as constraint
sections.summary: She completes the five-rule framework. Rule 3, asymmetric default: when unsure, hold and fix safety bugs but ship polish bugs. Rule 4, calibrate to revealed, not stated, risk tolerance, because the launch bar equals what production already accepts. Rule 5, humans are the constraint: judges scale, pattern interpretation does not, and fast-follows are committed debt rather than optional backlog. The framework tells you how to decide but assumes the underlying signal is true.

sections.title: Verify the scorer before you trust the score
sections.summary: In a non-deterministic system the judge is also non-deterministic. Before changing prompts because a clinical-accuracy judge drops from a steady 4.9 to 4.5, first ask whether the judge is right. A side-by-side example shows scenario A where the agent gives FDA-standard 400 mg caffeine guidance with pregnancy/medication context and the judge falsely flags hallucination (fix the judge), versus scenario B where the agent says 1,000 mg/day is fine and the judge correctly flags (fix the agent). Fixing a judge prompt is not cheating; judges are software that must continuously evolve.

sections.title: The whole talk in one slide
sections.summary: One-slide summary. Architecture pattern: don't X what you can Y, i.e., don't policy what you can architect, don't prompt what you can code, don't gate what you can monitor. Decisioning pattern: score by the worst case, default to the safer mistake, calibrate to your org, design for the human in the loop, and treat fast-follows as debt not backlog. Building guardrails first is slower than bolting them on later, but that is the design, not a limitation. Architecture is how, decisioning is when, member trust is why.

demonstrations: Member mentions of self-harm, suicidal ideation, or acute medical emergency routed to 911/988 by code before the model sees the turn.
Deterministic intent routing across clinical, tech support, education, and exercise recommendation capabilities.
Identity verification / authentication enforced as a security boundary before any member-data touch.
Random sample traces across capabilities with 100% sampling on high-stake cases.
Five-stakeholder disagreement over a feature 5 days before launch, with clinical, legal, compliance, product, and engineering seeing five different risks.

Side-by-side judge verification: scenario A, agent gives FDA-standard 400 mg caffeine guidance plus pregnancy/medication context, judge falsely flags hallucination (fix the judge); scenario B, agent says 1,000 mg/day is fine, judge correctly flags (fix the agent).
Steady clinical-accuracy judge score dropping from 4.9 to 4.5 over two days triggers a verify-the-scorer investigation before any prompt changes.
limitations: Even with continuous monitoring, the failure rate never hits zero and each fix round buys less under new prompts, tools, and model shifts.
Probabilistic models are unreliable for behaviors that cannot ever be wrong, so such decisions must be offloaded to deterministic code.
Most healthcare AI safety failures are architectural, not model capability, so better models alone do not fix them.
Judges themselves are non-deterministic software, so a judge-score drop can reflect judge drift rather than agent drift.

organization.name: Hinge Health
organization.summary: Hinge Health, Inc. (NYSE: HNGE) is an independent San Francisco digital musculoskeletal clinic. Its first-party site describes virtual physical therapy, a dedicated care team, and an AI care assistant (Robin) with computer-vision Movement Analysis. Official About and AI-principles pages document member-centered, privacy-preserving AI that complements clinicians. Rashi Agrawal leads AI and ML and presents Hinge Health's architectural guardrails for member-facing health AI. ECRI is a cited hazard-ranking authority, not the implementation owner.
organization.status: Independent public company as of the research date. Homepage, employer product page, AI-principles page, and 2025 AI-tools press release are live. No ownership change since the August 2026 talk.

evidence.excerpt: A 60-year-old healthy man asked a popular AI assistant how to cut salt from his diet. The LLM told him to swap it with bromine sodium bromide. He did it for 3 months. He landed in the ER with paranoia and hallucinations. Bromide levels 200 times the safe limit. 3 weeks in the hospital.
evidence.supports: Concrete real-world example of a consumer AI causing serious medical harm by giving unsafe diet advice.

evidence.excerpt: The first independent safety test of a consumer health AI out of Mount Sinai found that this health AI is under triaging life-threatening emergency 50% of the times.
evidence.supports: Independent academic safety test showing under-triaging of life-threatening emergencies in ~50% of cases.

evidence.excerpt: ECRI the patient safety group that hospitals trust to rank their top risks named AI chatbot misuse as the number one health technology hazard of 2026.
evidence.supports: Independent patient-safety authority ranking AI chatbot misuse as the top 2026 health-technology hazard.

evidence.excerpt: 40 million people actually use these models for triaging their health care issues.
evidence.supports: Scale of self-triaging behavior motivating the talk.

evidence.excerpt: The architecture version strips PHI at the pipeline boundary. At ingestion before it ever reaches the data lake. By the time the data is stored, the PHI is gone. So, a developer opens a dashboard there's nothing to redact.
evidence.supports: Architectural PHI protection by stripping at ingestion so nothing needs redacting downstream.

evidence.excerpt: Must not fail behavior belongs above your prompt, above the model. ... there is a code layer that runs first on every turn before the model even runs.
evidence.supports: Deterministic code layer above the model for never-wrong decisions.

evidence.excerpt: Even the labs that be build these frontier models publish the authority hierarchy. Root, system, developer, user, guideline. Every layer above user is one prompt injection away from being overridden.
evidence.supports: Frontier labs' own authority hierarchy shows prompts are not a security boundary.

evidence.excerpt: If a member mentions self-harm, suicidal ideation, or an acute medical emergency, the system must route to 911 or 988. The model should not even see this turn. Code runs first, decides, and routes, and makes a decision right away.
evidence.supports: Emergency escalation routed deterministically before the model sees the turn.

evidence.excerpt: Safety is not a gate you pass once. It is a continuous layer that runs the whole time. Most teams treat evals as a pre-launch checklist. ... judges that continuously keep scoring real conversations as they happen.
evidence.supports: Safety as continuous live-traffic judging, not a pre-launch gate.

evidence.excerpt: Some failures you can't just prompt away. You ship the fix, it comes back under new conditions. ... Each round buys you less and less. The rate never hits zero. ... A new failure that you see in production simply means you now have a new judge.
evidence.supports: Production failures regress under new conditions, so each new failure becomes a new judge.

evidence.excerpt: Five stakeholders look at the same issue. Each one sees a different risk. ... Clinical sees member safety risk. Legal sees regulatory exposure. Compliance sees audit risk. Product sees adoption risk. Engineering sees velocity risk.
evidence.supports: Five-stakeholder launch decisioning scenario with five distinct risks.

evidence.excerpt: A bug that lightly annoys 100% of users is way less severe than one that could cause serious harm in 0.1% of cases. ... the worst case matters more than the average case, always.
evidence.supports: Rule 1: worst-plausible-case severity sets priority, with a 0.1% serious-harm example.
